title: Pseudodeterministic NC perfect matching in general graphs
formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized family of Boolean circuits of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth that finds a perfect matching in every labeled general graph pseudodeterministically? Precisely, do there exist constants \(a,b,C\ge1\), a logspace-uniform family \((A_n)_{n\ge1}\), and a fixed selector \(F\) on all finite labeled simple undirected graphs, such that \(A_n\) has at most \(C(n+2)^a\) gates and random input bits, depth at most \(C\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^b\), and \[ \forall G\text{ on }[n]:\quad \Pr_r[A_n(G,r)=F(G)]\ge2/3?\] The selector outputs one perfect matching of \(G\) when one exists and a distinguished failure value otherwise.
why: Reproducible output is a basic distinction between randomized search and pseudodeterministic computation. Resolving this question for general perfect matching extends a central parallel graph problem beyond bipartite structure while retaining one overwhelmingly repeatable answer for each input.
status_note: Resolved by Anari and Vazirani, ITCS 2020, Corollary 3; the publisher PDF’s theorem, corollary and explanatory paragraph were checked against the 2017 source target. ITCS 2026 Article 4 independently attributes the non-bipartite extension to that work. The scope includes the unweighted labeled-graph target here. This is a source-based resolution audit, not a full independent re-verification of the matching algorithm or a Lean-certified benchmark submission.

importance.reason: A broad historical derandomization milestone for parallel search on a central graph problem. Pseudodeterminism is substantially stronger than ordinary randomized matching and is distinct from the unresolved deterministic general matching target.

sentences: A randomized parallel algorithm must output the same selected perfect matching on almost every run of a fixed input graph.
The source established this guarantee for bipartite graphs and asked for general non-bipartite graphs.
The resource target is polynomial circuit size and polylogarithmic depth with an effective uniform construction.
Anari and Vazirani’s published 2020 result gives the required pseudodeterministic algorithm even for polynomially weighted general graphs.
The historical question is retired as resolved while retaining its source record and the distinction from deterministic matching in NC.

definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), and the graph is specified by its \(n\times n\) Boolean adjacency matrix, required to be symmetric with zero diagonal. No bipartite, planar, degree or weight promise is imposed. A perfect matching is a set of edges in which each vertex occurs exactly once. Its output encoding is one success flag followed by one bit for each unordered pair \(u<v\), in lexicographic order, identifying the selected edges. The failure value is the zero flag followed by all zero bits. It is the required selector value exactly when no perfect matching exists.

Each \(A_n\) is an acyclic Boolean circuit with fan-in at most two AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, constants, adjacency input bits, and a finite number of independent unbiased random input bits. Circuit size counts computational gates; the separately stated polynomial bound also applies to the number of random inputs and the output length. Depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. Every random assignment induces a finite evaluation with these same resource bounds. There is no oracle gate, advice string, or graph-dependent preprocessing.

Logspace uniformity means that one deterministic Turing transducer, on unary input \(1^n\), outputs the complete description of \(A_n\), including its wiring and the input/output conventions, using \(O(\log(n+2))\) working cells. The transducer has a read-only input tape and a write-only output tape; every output bit is generated effectively. The size, depth and uniformity constants are independent of the graph and \(n\).

The selector \(F(G)\) is fixed before the random bits are drawn. It may depend on the entire labeled graph and on the chosen circuit family; no particular lexicographically least matching is prescribed, and no efficient independent procedure computing \(F\) is assumed. Consistent output under relabeling is not required. The probability statement requires equality of the entire output to this one value, rather than merely that most runs produce some valid matching. On the remaining probability mass the circuit may produce any bit string. The condition on graphs without a perfect matching is the usual totalization by a failure value; the substantive search target concerns graphs that have one.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of the stated uniform family and selector, including the all-input probability and size/depth bounds, or prove their nonexistence. An algorithm whose successful runs can choose unrelated matchings does not establish pseudodeterminism. A deterministic polylogarithmic-depth reduction with an unresolved oracle does not by itself meet the target; the final family must have only the listed Boolean gates and random inputs. No isomorphism-invariant canonical labeling is required.

context_blocks.text: Goldwasser and Grossman showed that a randomized parallel algorithm can repeatedly select the same matching of a fixed bipartite graph with high probability. Their concluding question explicitly asks for the analogous guarantee on general graphs. “Pseudo-deterministic NC” in that source allows randomness; it does not mean deterministic NC.

The output guarantee concerns the labeled graph supplied to the algorithm. A graph may have many perfect matchings, but the algorithm must concentrate on one selected matching across runs. It need not choose the same abstract matching after an arbitrary relabeling, so the question does not impose graph canonization.

Anari and Vazirani’s published Corollary 3 supplies a pseudodeterministic randomized NC algorithm for minimum-weight perfect matching in general graphs with polynomially bounded weights. The unweighted target is included. Their preceding theorem uses a weighted-decision oracle, but the corollary is an unconditional randomized algorithm; retaining the oracle would misstate the result.

The 2026 minimum-cut paper explicitly cites this general-graph extension as an established predecessor. The historical open question is therefore retired with its original provenance. This disposition concerns the literature result, and does not certify a Lean implementation or a solution of deterministic general-graph matching in NC.
